claims.claim: DESCRIBE HISTORY, VERSION AS OF, versionAsOf, RESTORE TABLE and OPTIMIZE ... ZORDER BY work; RESTORE creates a new version; VACUUM RETAIN 0 HOURS fails the safety check.
claims.source: Run on delta-spark 4.0.1 in this repository.

claims.claim: deletedFileRetentionDuration defaults to 7 days and logRetentionDuration to 30 days; from Databricks Runtime 18.0 time travel beyond deletedFileRetentionDuration is blocked.
Databricks recommends liquid clustering and predictive optimization for Unity Catalog managed tables.

concept_html:
Every Delta write creates a new table version. The transaction log keeps the list, and you can read any version still on storage.

  • DESCRIBE HISTORY t lists versions with the operation, user and metrics.
  • spark.read.option("versionAsOf", 12).table("t") or SELECT * FROM t VERSION AS OF 12 reads an old version. timestampAsOf and TIMESTAMP AS OF work by time.
  • RESTORE TABLE t TO VERSION AS OF 12 makes version 12 current again, as a new version. History is kept, so you can undo the restore.

Time travel is your first response to a bad write: compare the versions, restore, then fix the job.

Two maintenance commands keep tables fast and storage bounded.

OPTIMIZE compacts many small files into fewer large ones. Frequent small appends leave thousands of tiny files, and every query pays to open them. OPTIMIZE t ZORDER BY (wave_id) also co-locates rows by a column. On Unity Catalog managed tables, Databricks recommends liquid clustering (CLUSTER BY, or CLUSTER BY AUTO) with predictive optimization, which runs OPTIMIZE and VACUUM for you.

VACUUM deletes data files that no current version needs and that are older than the retention window. The window comes from delta.deletedFileRetentionDuration, which defaults to 7 days. Delta blocks VACUUM t RETAIN 0 HOURS with a safety check, because a running reader or writer might still need those files.

VACUUM limits time travel. After it runs, versions whose files it removed can no longer be read. The log itself keeps entries for delta.logRetentionDuration, 30 days by default. From Databricks Runtime 18.0, time travel beyond deletedFileRetentionDuration is blocked outright. If you need 30 days of recoverable history, set both properties to at least 30 days.

lines: -- 1. Find the last good version.
DESCRIBE HISTORY research_gold.nat_metrics;
SELECT wave_id, SUM(weighted_base) AS base
FROM research_gold.nat_metrics VERSION AS OF 41
GROUP BY wave_id;
-- 3. Restore. This writes a new version, so it can be undone.
RESTORE TABLE research_gold.nat_metrics TO VERSION AS OF 41;
ALTER TABLE research_gold.nat_metrics SET TBLPROPERTIES (
'delta.deletedFileRetentionDuration' = 'interval 30 days',
'delta.logRetentionDuration' = 'interval 30 days'

example.takeaway_html: History turns a data incident into a two-minute restore. Keep it long enough to be useful.

lines: SET spark.databricks.delta.retentionDurationCheck.enabled = false;
VACUUM research_gold.nat_metrics RETAIN 0 HOURS;
-- gold was overwritten by mistake last night; rebuild everything
DROP TABLE research_gold.nat_metrics;

notes.html: Switches off the safety check that exists to stop the next line.
Deletes every unreferenced file now. Time travel and RESTORE no longer work.
With history intact, a RESTORE takes seconds. Dropping and rebuilding takes hours.

title: Time travel, RESTORE, OPTIMIZE and VACUUM
why_html:
A developer runs a gold rebuild against the wrong wave filter and overwrites three weeks of metrics. The team wants to restore, but a clean-up job ran VACUUM ... RETAIN 0 HOURS nightly, with the retention check switched off "to save storage". The overwritten files are gone. Three weeks of gold are rebuilt from silver overnight, and two client extracts go out late.

With the default 7-day retention, RESTORE TABLE research_gold.nat_metrics TO VERSION AS OF the last good version takes seconds.
